newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-RED WINGS REAP BOUNTY OF SHANAHAN TRADE IN FINALS.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-RED WINGS REAP BOUNTY OF SHANAHAN TRADE IN FINALS.

text.p: Red Wings coach Scotty Bowman told Brendan Shanahan that he needed more offence from the sharpshooter he acquired to help his team win the Stanley Cup this season, and the Detroit winger responded to the pressure big time on Tuesday.

Flying at a separate altitude that most of his teammates -- not to mention his opponents -- Shanahan scored two goals in Game 2 of the championship series to lead his team to a 4-2 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers as Detroit seized a 2-0 lead in the best-of-seven series for hockey's Holy Grail.

Freed from hockey limbo in Hartford in October after playing for a team that rarely makes the playoffs and never contends for the Stanley Cup, Shanahan scored 47 goals in the regular season for Detroit.
But he had been surprisingly quiet in the first three rounds of the playoffs, scoring just five times in Detroit's first 15 post-season contests.

When Bowman asked for more in the late stages of the Western Conference finals against the defending champion Colorado Avalanche, Shanahan iced the clinching win with an empty net goal in a 3-1 victory that propelled the two-time 50-goal scorer into the promised land of the first Stanley Cup finals of his 10-year NHL career.
"He has had a lot of pressure on him. There has been a lot of pressure on Brendan Shanahan, and he has responded," said Detroit coach Scotty Bowman.
Shanahan, 28, who looked sharp in Game 1 against Philadelphia, really turned his game up a few notches Tuesday.

He started the game like he had been cut loose from a prison chain gang, ripping through several Flyers' checks and careening around the ice in his first shift when the puck wound up on his stick at centre ice.

Carrying the puck into the Flyers zone over the left wing and gathering a serious head of steam, Shanahan let rip a long shot that ticked off defenceman Paul Coffey's skate and beat goaltender Garth Snow.
The goal, just 97 seconds into the game, came on Detroit's first shot on goal and set the tone for the rest of the contest.

Shanahan missed a golden opportunity to practically put the game out of reach in the first period on a breakaway attempt that could have put his team ahead 3-0. He appeared to have Snow beat but, the puck bounced off the goal post.
"I was just trying to settle the puck down. I guess I muffed it," he said, almost apologetically.

But he made up for it with another goal at 9:56 of the third period, completing a 2-on-1 break with Martin Lapointe that restored his team's two-goal lead and effectively took the Flyers out of the game.
Shanahan knows what his former teammates on the Hartford Whalers feel like.
"It's horrible to be sitting down and not involved. That's not what we're trained to do," he said.
The pressure of competing for the Stanley Cup in June when players from 24 other teams are fishing or on the golf course is something to be savored.
"I think that's part of pro sports -- pressure," a delighted Shanahan said.
"It's better than not facing any pressure. If you have the mentality and you're the kind of person that wants to become a professional athlete, you enjoy pressure."

Only two teams in Stanley Cup history have lost the first two games of the series on home ice and come back to win the Stanley Cup -- the 1942 Toronto Maple Leafs and 1966 Montreal Canadiens. Each time the opposing team was the Red Wings.
But if the Flyers are going to take heart from that they had better realise that nither of those Detroit teams had Brendan Shanahan on the roster.
